title: The Weirdest Roman Emperors
description:
A pee tax, an emperor found hiding behind a curtain, a man who bought the empire at an auction, a teenage priest with a sacred rock, an Olympic champion who fell out of his chariot, a war on seashells, and an emperor who thought he was Hercules: seven of the weirdest Roman emperors, counted down from seven to one. Every story comes from real ancient sources, and we flag the gossip and the legends. Chapters are added automatically.

#history #romanempire #ancientrome #funnyhistory #historypros

beats.say: Rome, 192 AD. Tens of thousands of people pack the Colosseum to watch a gladiator fight.
And the gladiator walking out onto the sand is... the emperor of Rome.
Who's ready to watch me win again?
In the front rows sit the senators, Rome's top politicians. They have to cheer whatever they're told to cheer.
One of them, a senator named Cassius Dio, is trying very, very hard not to laugh.
And honestly? This isn't even the only weird thing a Roman emperor ever did.
Today we're counting down seven of the weirdest Roman emperors. Commodus is number one.
Quick warning: many of these stories come from Roman writers like Suetonius, who loved gossip and often hated the emperors. When a story is probably a legend, we'll say so.

show.sub: Seven emperors. All real. Deeply strange.

beats.say: Number seven: Vespasian, the emperor who put a tax on pee.
He was a tough old soldier who won a civil war in 69 AD. The prize? An empire that was totally broke.

show.label: Rome's treasury when Vespasian took over
show.sub: after Nero's spending and a year of civil war

beats.say: Now, Romans collected pee from public toilets. Laundries used it to clean clothes, and tanners used it to soften leather.
So Vespasian taxed it. His son Titus was disgusted.
Dad, a tax on pee? That's disgusting.
Smell this coin. Does it stink?
No?
And yet it comes from pee.
That's where we get the saying "money doesn't stink". And he kept joking to the end. When he fell sick for the last time, in 79 AD, Suetonius says he said this.
Woe's me. Methinks I'm turning into a god.

show.text: Woe's me. Methinks I'm turning into a god.
show.who: Vespasian, falling ill for the last time, 79 AD (Suetonius, Life of Vespasian 23, trans. J. C. Rolfe)

beats.say: Rome often declared dead emperors to be gods. So yes, he was joking about his own death.
Oh, and this penny-pinching pee taxer also started building the Colosseum.

show.title: The Emperor Found Behind a Curtain

beats.say: Number six: Claudius, who got the top job by hiding.
Claudius was the uncle of the emperor Caligula. He limped and stammered, so his own family treated him as a joke and kept him away from power.
Then, in 41 AD, guards killed Caligula inside the palace. Claudius panicked and hid behind a curtain on a balcony.
A guard noticed a pair of feet sticking out. The historian Josephus even gives his name: Gratus.
Hey! I know you. You're Claudius!
Please! Don't hurt me!
Hurt you? You're our new emperor!
The guards carried him to their camp and declared him emperor. He was fifty years old.

show.label: Claudius's age when he became emperor
show.sub: after a lifetime of being ignored

beats.say: But the man everyone ignored was actually a serious scholar. He had written history books about the Etruscans and Carthage.
And the family joke was actually good at the job. Two years later, his army invaded Britain, and he went to see it himself.

show.title: The Man Who Bought the Empire

beats.say: Number five: Didius Julianus, who bought the whole Roman Empire at an auction.
In March 193, the Praetorian Guard, the emperor's own bodyguards, killed the emperor Pertinax. He'd been trying to make them behave.
Then the guards had a brilliant idea. Why not sell the job to whoever paid the most?
Two rich men bid in sesterces, Roman coins. Sulpicianus, the dead emperor's father-in-law, was inside the camp. Julianus shouted his offers from outside the wall.
Twenty thousand sesterces for every soldier!
Twenty-five thousand!
Sold! For every guard, that was about twenty years of a regular soldier's pay. Cassius Dio, who lived through it, tells the whole story.

show.label: Julianus's winning bid
show.sub: sesterces per guard: about 20 years of a regular soldier's pay

beats.say: The people of Rome hated it. They shouted insults at him in the streets.
Worse, Roman generals with real armies refused to accept him. One of them, Septimius Severus, marched on Rome.
After just sixty-six days, Julianus was killed in his own palace. Dio says his last words were: but what evil have I done?
Turns out you can buy a throne. You just can't buy anyone's respect.
Number four: Elagabalus, who became emperor at fourteen.
He was a teenage priest of a sun god from Emesa, a city in Syria. His powerful grandmother, Julia Maesa, got the army to make him emperor.
And when he moved to Rome, he brought his god with him: a big black stone, maybe a meteorite.
He built it a giant temple on the Palatine Hill, and put his sun god above Jupiter, Rome's king of the gods.
The Romans were not amused. Swapping out the gods was a very big deal.
There's a famous legend about him, too. It says he dropped so many violets and other flowers on his dinner guests, from a trick ceiling, that some couldn't climb out.
That comes from the Historia Augusta, a Roman book so full of made-up stories that historians barely trust it. A famous painting from 1888 even swapped the violets for roses.
What's not a legend: in 222, his own guards turned on him. He was eighteen.

show.title: The Emperor Who Fell Off and Still Won

beats.say: Number three: Nero, the emperor who wanted to be a rock star.
Nero loved to sing while playing the lyre, a small harp. And he made sure everybody listened.
On a tour of Greece, Suetonius says, nobody was allowed to leave his shows. Some people faked being dead, just to be carried out.
On that same tour, in 66 AD, one listener kept nodding off: an old general named Vespasian. Yes, the pee tax guy.
Excuse me. Are you sleeping during my song?
What? No! Bravo! Beautiful!
Nero kicked him out of his court. Bad move: Vespasian would end up ruling Rome.
In Greece, Nero also entered the Olympic Games. The Games were even rescheduled so he could compete.
He drove a chariot pulled by ten horses. He fell out, got back in, and gave up before the finish line.
The judges crowned him the winner anyway.

show.label: Nero's Olympic chariot race
show.sub: fell out, didn't finish, still won

beats.say: And did he fiddle while Rome burned in 64 AD? No. Fiddles didn't exist yet, and the historian Tacitus says Nero was at Antium, about fifty kilometers away, when the fire started.
Number two: Caligula, who became emperor in 37 AD, at just twenty-four.
Ancient writers describe a spoiled ruler. His favorite racehorse, Incitatus, reportedly had a marble stall and an ivory food box.
Rumor even said he planned to make the horse a consul, one of Rome's two top officials. That's probably gossip, or a joke to insult the Senate.
But my favorite Caligula story is this one. In 40 AD, he marched his army to the coast of Gaul, which is now France, facing Britain.
The soldiers lined up for battle. Trumpets blared. Everybody waited for the invasion.
Then, Suetonius says, Caligula ordered them to pick up seashells, and fill their helmets with them.
He called them the spoils of the Ocean, owed to Rome. Victory over... the sea.
Some historians think the Latin word used, musculi, could also mean army work huts. So this might be a mix-up. Either way, there was no invasion.
Britain had to wait three more years, for the man behind the curtain.

show.title: The Emperor Who Thought He Was Hercules

beats.say: And number one: Commodus, the emperor who decided he was Hercules.
His father was Marcus Aurelius, one of Rome's wisest emperors. Commodus took over alone in 180, at eighteen. He's the bad guy in the movie Gladiator.
He said he was Hercules, the legendary Greek hero, reborn. He wore a lion skin and carried a club.
He renamed all twelve months of the year after his own names and titles.
He even had a giant bronze statue near the Colosseum redone as himself, as Hercules. And he renamed the city of Rome. It was now the Colony of Commodus.
And he fought in the arena. Dio says he paid himself a million sesterces from the gladiator fund for every day he fought.
Which brings us back to Dio in the stands. One day, Commodus hunted an ostrich, then marched over to the senators, holding up its head, as if to say: you're next.
He didn't say a word. He just grinned at them.
Dio says he pulled leaves off his laurel wreath and chewed them, so nobody could see him laughing.
It didn't end well. On the last day of 192, Commodus was murdered by his own people. And that chaos is what led to the auction of Didius Julianus.
Honorable mention: Caracalla. In 212 AD he made almost every free person in the empire a Roman citizen. Sounds generous! Cassius Dio says the real goal was more taxes.
That's the list: a pee taxer, a man behind a curtain, an empire buyer, a teenage priest, a champion who didn't finish, a seashell general, and Hercules.
Which emperor was the weirdest? Tell us in the comments.
